claim: Primate TRIM5α uses its rapidly evolving 'v1' loop to bind retroviral capsids.
source: For example, primate TRIM5α uses its rapidly evolving 'v1' loop to bind retroviral capsids, and single mutations in this loop can dramatically improve retroviral restriction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about TRIM5α function.

claim: Single mutations in the TRIM5α v1 loop can dramatically improve retroviral restriction.
source: For example, primate TRIM5α uses its rapidly evolving 'v1' loop to bind retroviral capsids, and single mutations in this loop can dramatically improve retroviral restriction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The majority of mutations in the TRIM5α v1 loop increase weak antiviral function.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the majority of mutations increase weak antiviral function.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deep mutational scanning experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Most random mutations do not disrupt potent viral restriction by TRIM5α, even when newly acquired via a single adaptive substitution.
source: Moreover, most random mutations do not disrupt potent viral restriction, even when it is newly acquired via a single adaptive substitution.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the deep mutational scanning experiments on TRIM5α-R332P and rhesus TRIM5α.

claim: TRIM5α's adaptive landscape is remarkably broad and mutationally resilient.
source: Our results indicate that TRIM5α's adaptive landscape is remarkably broad and mutationally resilient, maximizing its chances of success in evolutionary arms races with retroviruses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the deep mutational scanning data.

claim: Mammalian genomes encode cell-intrinsic antiviral proteins termed restriction factors that recognize and inhibit viral replication.
source: Mammalian genomes combat the persistent threat of viruses by encoding a battery of cell-intrinsic antiviral proteins, termed restriction factors, that recognize and inhibit viral replication within host cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about innate immunity.

claim: Viral escape from restriction factors spurs adaptation of restriction factors by selecting for variants that re-establish viral recognition.
source: In turn, viral escape spurs adaptation of restriction factors, by selecting for variants that re-establish viral recognition and thereby restriction (McCarthy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCarthy et al., 2015.

claim: Mutual antagonism between viruses and hosts drives cycles of recurrent adaptation in prey-predator-like genetic arms races.
source: Mutual antagonism between viruses and their hosts thus drives cycles of recurrent adaptation, in prey-predator-like genetic arms races (Van Valen, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Van Valen, 1973.

claim: Arms races between viruses and hosts result in rapid evolution of restriction factors, which accumulate amino acid mutations at virus-binding interfaces at a higher than expected rate.
source: These arms races result in the rapid evolution of restriction factors, which accumulate amino acid mutations at their virus-binding interfaces at a higher than expected rate (Daugherty and Malik, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daugherty and Malik, 2012.

claim: TRIM5α evolves rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
source: Numerous restriction factors, including TRIM5α (Sawyer et al., 2005), APOBEC3G (Sawyer et al., 2004), and MxA (Mitchell et al., 2012), evolve rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2005.

claim: APOBEC3G evolves rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
source: Numerous restriction factors, including TRIM5α (Sawyer et al., 2005), APOBEC3G (Sawyer et al., 2004), and MxA (Mitchell et al., 2012), evolve rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2004.

claim: MxA evolves rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
source: Numerous restriction factors, including TRIM5α (Sawyer et al., 2005), APOBEC3G (Sawyer et al., 2004), and MxA (Mitchell et al., 2012), evolve rapidly as a result of arms races with target viruses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2012.

claim: Divergence between restriction factor orthologs can result in cross-species barriers to viral infection.
source: The resulting divergence between restriction factor orthologs can result in cross-species barriers to viral infection (Compton and Emerman, 2013; Kirmaier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Compton and Emerman, 2013 and Kirmaier et al., 2010.

claim: Rhesus TRIM5α potently restricts HIV-1.
source: Rhesus TRIM5α could potently restrict HIV-1, whereas the virus almost completely escapes TRIM5α-mediated inhibition in its human host.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Stremlau et al., 2004.

claim: HIV-1 almost completely escapes TRIM5α-mediated inhibition in humans.
source: Rhesus TRIM5α could potently restrict HIV-1, whereas the virus almost completely escapes TRIM5α-mediated inhibition in its human host.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Stremlau et al., 2004.

claim: Restriction of SIVs varies across TRIM5α orthologs.
source: Subsequent studies revealed that restriction of SIVs (simian immunodeficiency viruses) also varies across TRIM5α orthologs and that SIVs likely drove the rapid evolution of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys (McCarthy et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCarthy et al., 2015 and Wu et al., 2013.

claim: SIVs likely drove the rapid evolution of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys.
source: Subsequent studies revealed that restriction of SIVs (simian immunodeficiency viruses) also varies across TRIM5α orthologs and that SIVs likely drove the rapid evolution of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys (McCarthy et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCarthy et al., 2015 and Wu et al., 2013.

claim: TRIM5α disrupts retroviral replication early in infection by binding to the capsid core of retroviruses entering the cell.
source: TRIM5α disrupts retroviral replication early in infection by binding to the capsid core of retroviruses entering the cell (Li et al., 2016; Maillard et al., 2007; Owens et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016, Maillard et al., 2007, and Owens et al., 2003.

claim: TRIM5α binding to the capsid causes premature uncoating of the viral core, preventing delivery of the viral genome to the nucleus for integration.
source: Its binding causes the premature uncoating of the viral core (Stremlau et al., 2006), preventing delivery of the viral genome to the nucleus for integration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stremlau et al., 2006.

claim: TRIM5α binds to the capsid via the unstructured v1 loop within its B30.2 domain.
source: TRIM5α binds to the capsid via the unstructured v1 loop within its B30.2 domain (Biris et al., 2012; Sebastian and Luban, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biris et al., 2012 and Sebastian and Luban, 2005.

claim: The v1 loop is critical for recognition of capsid from many retroviruses.
source: Experiments swapping the v1 loop between TRIM5α orthologs indicated that it is critical for recognition of capsid from many retroviruses (Ohkura et al., 2006; Perron et al., 2006; Sawyer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohkura et al., 2006, Perron et al., 2006, and Sawyer et al., 2005.

claim: Rapid evolution of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys and hominoids is concentrated within the v1 loop.
source: In Old World monkeys and hominoids, rapid evolution of TRIM5α is concentrated within this v1 loop (Sawyer et al., 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2005 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Single amino acid mutations at rapidly evolving sites in the v1 loop can cause dramatic gains of restriction against HIV-1 and other retroviruses.
source: Single amino acid mutations at these rapidly evolving sites can cause dramatic gains of restriction against HIV-1 and other retroviruses (Li et al., 2006; Maillard et al., 2007; Yap et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2006, Maillard et al., 2007, and Yap et al., 2005.

claim: Primate TRIM5α orthologs have sampled relatively limited amino acid diversity at rapidly evolving positions within the v1 loop.
source: Despite their rapid evolution, primate TRIM5α orthologs have sampled relatively limited amino acid diversity at rapidly evolving positions within the capsid-binding v1 loop (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A alignment.

claim: Single amino acid changes at residue 332 are responsible for dramatic differences in antiviral restriction.
source: For example, although single amino acid changes at residue 332 are responsible for dramatic differences in antiviral restriction (Li et al., 2006), this residue repeatedly toggles between just three amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Residue 332 in TRIM5α repeatedly toggles between just three amino acids during evolution.
source: For example, although single amino acid changes at residue 332 are responsible for dramatic differences in antiviral restriction (Li et al., 2006), this residue repeatedly toggles between just three amino acids.
evidence: This is observed from the alignment in Figure 1A.

claim: Most amino acids that can be sampled with single nucleotide changes are not observed among primate TRIM5α orthologs.
source: The limited diversity is not due to evolutionary inaccessibility, since most amino acids that can be sampled with single nucleotide changes are not observed among primate TRIM5α orthologs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A deep mutational scanning library of all single amino acid variants within the v1 loop (amino acids 330 to 340) was generated with a library diversity of 231 amino acid (352 nucleotide) variants.
source: We first generated a library of all single amino acid variants (including stop codons) within the rapidly evolving portion of the v1 loop (amino acids 330 to 340, Figure 1A), with a library diversity of 231 amino acid (352 nucleotide) variants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CRFK cells naturally lack TRIM5α.
source: The resulting TRIM5α variants were stably expressed via transduction into CRFK (cat renal fibroblast) cells, which naturally lack TRIM5α (McEwan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McEwan et al., 2009.

claim: Enrichment scores were highly correlated between two independent biological replicates (Spearman r = 0.97).
source: Enrichment scores were highly correlated between two independent biological replicates (Figure 2C, Spearman r = 0.97).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutants bearing premature stop codons were all among the most depleted variants in the HIV-1 restrictor pool.
source: Furthermore, mutants bearing premature stop codons, which should be non-functional and depleted from the restrictor pool, were all among the most depleted variants (Figure 2D, red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wildtype human TRIM5α weakly restricts HIV-1 (~2 fold).
source: Despite the weak (~2 fold) restriction of HIV-1 by wildtype (WT) human TRIM5α, variants containing synonymous nucleotide changes (no amino acid changes compared to WT, blue) had significantly higher enrichment scores than those containing stop codons (p<0.0001, student's unpaired t-test with Welch's correction), confirming that the assay worked as expected.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the validation of the assay.

claim: Enrichment scores and fold-restriction were highly correlated across all mutants tested (Spearman r = 0.90).
source: Indeed, enrichment scores and fold-restriction were highly correlated across all mutants tested (Spearman r = 0.90).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: More than half of all missense variants (115, 57%) had enrichment scores that fell more than two standard deviations above WT TRIM5α.
source: Contrary to this expectation, we found that more than half of all missense variants (115, 57%) had enrichment scores that fell more than two standard deviations above WT TRIM5α (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Among evolutionarily accessible amino acid variants (via single-nucleotide changes from WT), 54% (32 variants) had enrichment scores more than two standard deviations above WT TRIM5α.
source: Even if we limited our analysis to amino acid variants that are evolutionarily accessible via single-nucleotide changes from the WT TRIM5α sequence, this ratio did not change substantially (32, 54%).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The R332P variant of human TRIM5α improves HIV-1 restriction ~15 fold relative to WT (33-fold restriction).
source: These enrichment scores represent dramatic gains in HIV-1 restriction, with the most potent variants (R332P and R335A) improving HIV-1 restriction ~15 fold relative to WT (33- and 39-fold restriction, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The R335A variant of human TRIM5α improves HIV-1 restriction ~15 fold relative to WT (39-fold restriction).
source: These enrichment scores represent dramatic gains in HIV-1 restriction, with the most potent variants (R332P and R335A) improving HIV-1 restriction ~15 fold relative to WT (33- and 39-fold restriction, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Most gains in HIV-1 restriction by human TRIM5α variants could be completely accounted for by a reduction in the electrostatic charge of the v1 loop.
source: In contrast, most gains in HIV-1 restriction could be completely accounted for by a reduction in the electrostatic charge of the v1 loop (Figure 3A), regardless of expression level.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and stated in the text.

claim: Mutation of positively-charged residues 332 or 335 from arginine to any amino acid except lysine significantly improved HIV-1 restriction.
source: Among all variants tested, mutation of the positively-charged residues 332 or 335 from the WT arginine (R) to any amino acid except lysine (K) significantly improved HIV-1 restriction (Figure 3A–B), consistent with previous reports on R332 variants (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A-B and supported by citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Mutation of uncharged sites to K or R decreased TRIM5α restriction of HIV-1.
source: Mutation of uncharged sites to K or R decreased TRIM5α restriction of HIV-1, whereas introducing a negatively charged aspartic acid (D) or glutamic acid (E) significantly increased HIV-1 restriction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Introducing negatively charged aspartic acid (D) or glutamic acid (E) at uncharged sites significantly increased HIV-1 restriction.
source: Mutation of uncharged sites to K or R decreased TRIM5α restriction of HIV-1, whereas introducing a negatively charged aspartic acid (D) or glutamic acid (E) significantly increased HIV-1 restriction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Positive charge in the v1 loop is the dominant impediment to HIV-1 restriction by human TRIM5α.
source: Thus, we conclude that positive charge in the v1 loop is the dominant impediment to HIV-1 restriction by human TRIM5α.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 3.

claim: Mutation of G333 to most other amino acids significantly improves human TRIM5α activity against HIV-1.
source: For example, despite its strict conservation in primate TRIM5α (Figure 1A), a glycine (G) at residue 333 compromises HIV-1 restriction. Mutation of G333 to most other amino acids significantly improves TRIM5α activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No double mutants tested increased HIV-1 restriction beyond that of R332P alone.
source: However, we found that no double mutants tested increased HIV-1 restriction beyond that of R332P alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Combination of R335E with R332P resulted in loss of protein expression and HIV-1 restriction.
source: Instead, combination of one gain-of-function variant (R335E) with R332P resulted in loss of protein expression and HIV-1 restriction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The charge-altering mutations R332P and R335A increased restriction of all lentiviruses tested, including HIV-2, SIVcpz, and SIVmac.
source: However, the charge-altering mutations R332P and R335A increased restriction of all lentiviruses we tested, including HIV-2, SIVcpz (SIV infecting chimpanzees), and SIVmac (SIV infecting rhesus macaques).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Introduction of negative charge (R332E, R335E, G330E, G333D, and G337D) selectively improved restriction of HIV-1, SIVcpz, and HIV-2 but not SIVmac.
source: Introduction of negative charge (R332E, R335E, G330E, G333D, and G337D) also selectively improved restriction of HIV-1, SIVcpz, and HIV-2 but not SIVmac.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Positive charge at positions 332 and 335 appears to be generally detrimental for lentiviral restriction.
source: Thus, positive charge at positions 332 and 335 appears to be generally detrimental for lentiviral restriction.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 4A.

claim: 65% of all missense variants in the human TRIM5α-R332P library fell within two standard deviations of WT (R332P) enrichment in the HIV-1 non-restrictor pool.
source: Indeed, we found that the majority of missense variants (65%) did not weaken HIV-1 restriction by the R332P variant of human TRIM5α (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Half of all missense mutations (125, 51%) in rhesus TRIM5α fell within two standard deviations of WT enrichment in the HIV-1 non-restrictor pool.
source: In contrast, half of all missense mutations (125, 51%) fell within two standard deviations of WT.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Among missense mutations accessible by single-nucleotide changes in rhesus TRIM5α, 55% (40 variants) fell within two standard deviations of WT enrichment in the HIV-1 non-restrictor pool.
source: Even missense mutations accessible by single-nucleotide changes reflected this pattern (40, 55%).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Enrichment scores for rhesus TRIM5α variants negatively correlate with antiviral potency (Spearman r = -0.81).
source: By re-testing individual variants, we confirmed that enrichment scores negatively correlate with antiviral potency (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The introduction of positive charge, particularly arginine, weakened HIV-1 inhibition by rhesus TRIM5α.
source: In both cases, the introduction of positive charge, particularly R, weakened HIV-1 inhibition (Figure 5D, compare to Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The introduction of bulky hydrophobic residues, including leucine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan, significantly impaired HIV-1 restriction by rhesus TRIM5α but did not affect the potency of human TRIM5α.
source: In contrast, the introduction of bulky hydrophobic residues, including leucine (L), phenylalanine (F), and tryptophan (W), significantly impaired HIV-1 restriction by rhesus TRIM5α but did not affect the potency of human TRIM5α.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 58% of all missense variants in rhesus TRIM5α had no effect on N-MLV restriction.
source: Similar to HIV-1 restriction, we found that most missense mutations (143, 58%) in rhesus TRIM5α were tolerated for N-MLV restriction (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Hydrophobic and especially aromatic residues at most positions in the v1 loop significantly decreased N-MLV restriction by rhesus TRIM5α.
source: In particular, hydrophobic and especially aromatic residues at most positions in the v1 loop significantly decreased N-MLV restriction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: N-MLV restriction by rhesus TRIM5α is insensitive to the introduction of positively charged residues.
source: However, N-MLV restriction is insensitive to the introduction of positively charged residues, which disrupt HIV-1 inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 92% of all variants (187) in human TRIM5α had no effect on N-MLV restriction.
source: Human TRIM5α restriction of N-MLV was even more resilient to mutation than rhesus TRIM5α. Almost all variants (187, 92%) had no effect on N-MLV restriction (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Human TRIM5α restricts N-MLV with >250 fold potency.
source: This extreme mutational resilience may reflect the massive potency (>250 fold restriction, data not shown) of human TRIM5α against N-MLV, and/or a decreased reliance on the v1 loop for N-MLV recognition by human TRIM5α (Perron et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: TRIM5α's adaptive landscape is remarkably broad and mutationally resilient, maximizing its chances of success in evolutionary arms races with retroviruses.
source: Thus, TRIM5α appears to evolve with low-cost, high-gain fitness landscapes that favor its success in co-evolutionary battles with rapidly evolving retroviruses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Cyclophilin A (CypA) protects the HIV-1 capsid from TRIM5α recognition.
source: Recent findings revealed that cyclophilin A (CypA) protects the HIV-1 capsid from TRIM5α recognition (Kim et al., 2019; Selyutina et al., 2020; Veillette et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2019, Selyutina et al., 2020, and Veillette et al., 2013.

claim: Positive charge in the v1 loop might impair an interaction between TRIM5α and the capsid's CypA-binding site via electrostatic repulsion.
source: Although structural studies currently lack sufficient resolution to observe the molecular details of the TRIM5α–capsid interaction, we speculate that positive charge in the v1 loop impairs an interaction between TRIM5α and the capsid's CypA-binding site via electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: The detrimental effect of positive charge might be accounted for by lowering TRIM5α expression level.
source: Alternatively, the detrimental effect of positive charge might largely be accounted for by lowering TRIM5α expression level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Increasing human TRIM5α expression has been shown to improve HIV-1 restriction.
source: Increasing human TRIM5α expression has been shown to improve HIV-1 restriction (Richardson et al., 2014), although we identified at least one mutation (V340H) that improved expression without increasing activity against HIV-1 and at least one mutation (G333D) that reduced positive charge and improved HIV-1 restriction without increasing expression level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2014 and data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Many v1 loop mutations improved human TRIM5α restriction of HIV-1 without impairing N-MLV antiviral function.
source: More broadly, we identified many v1 loop mutations that improved human TRIM5α restriction of HIV-1, and even other lentiviruses, without impairing N-MLV antiviral function (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: TRIM5α has been shown to induce some innate immune signaling even in the absence of infection.
source: For example, TRIM5α has been shown to induce some innate immune signaling even in the absence of infection (Lascano et al., 2016; Pertel et al., 2011; Tareen and Emerman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lascano et al., 2016, Pertel et al., 2011, and Tareen and Emerman, 2011.

claim: Many gain-of-antiviral-function mutations increased TRIM5α expression levels.
source: Many gain-of-antiviral-function mutations increased TRIM5α expression levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and this increased expression might increase aberrant signaling by TRIM5α, driving chronic immune activation that can be costly for the host (Ashley et al., 2012; Okin and Medzhitov, 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations to Ashley et al., 2012 and Okin and Medzhitov, 2012.

claim: TRIM5α's antiviral restriction displays remarkable mutational resilience across multiple orthologs and against two divergent retroviruses, with 51–92% of all possible missense variants retaining antiviral activity.
source: Our analyses uncovered a second unexpected, advantageous aspect of TRIM5α's evolutionary landscape: its antiviral restriction displays remarkable mutational resilience across multiple orthologs and against two divergent retroviruses. 51–92% of all possible missense variants retain antiviral activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is summarized in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: TRIM5α's permissive landscape contrasts with the relative inflexibility of ligand-binding domains in the core of evolutionarily conserved proteins.
source: TRIM5α's permissive landscape contrasts with the relative inflexibility of ligand-binding domains in the core of evolutionarily conserved proteins (Guo et al., 2004; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Suckow et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2004, McLaughlin et al., 2012, and Suckow et al., 1996.

claim: The use of flexible loops for viral ligand binding by TRIM5α and MxA grants rapidly evolving restriction factors mutational flexibility without significant risk of disrupting core protein structure.
source: The use of flexible loops for viral ligand binding by TRIM5α, as well as MxA (Mitchell et al., 2012), thus grants rapidly evolving restriction factors mutational flexibility without significant risk of disrupting core protein structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2012.

claim: TRIM5α's reliance on the v1 loop for specificity mirrors that of antibodies' dependence on complementarity-defining loops for antigen recognition.
source: Intriguingly, TRIM5α's reliance on the v1 loop for specificity mirrors that of antibodies' dependence on complementarity-defining loops for antigen recognition.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn by the authors.

claim: A high degree of mutational tolerance within complementarity-defining loops allows somatic hypermutation to significantly increase antibody-antigen affinity.
source: Indeed, a high degree of mutational tolerance within complementarity-defining loops allows somatic hypermutation to significantly increase antibody-antigen affinity (Daugherty et al., 2000; NISC Comparative Sequencing Program et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Daugherty et al., 2000 and NISC Comparative Sequencing Program et al., 2017.

claim: Mutational tolerance facilitates the evolution of de novo functions through the accumulation of neutral mutations.
source: Indeed, mutational tolerance has been shown to facilitate the evolution of de novo functions through the accumulation of neutral mutations (Draghi et al., 2010; Hayden et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Draghi et al., 2010 and Hayden et al., 2011.

claim: Extensive polymorphism within the v1 loop of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys results in diverse antiviral repertoires that have been maintained by balancing selection.
source: Although rare in human populations (Clarke et al., 2017), extensive polymorphism within the v1 loop of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys results in diverse antiviral repertoires that have been maintained by balancing selection (Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clarke et al., 2017 and Newman et al., 2006.

claim: TRIM5α polymorphism is rare in human populations.
source: Although rare in human populations (Clarke et al., 2017), extensive polymorphism within the v1 loop of TRIM5α in Old World monkeys results in diverse antiviral repertoires that have been maintained by balancing selection (Newman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clarke et al., 2017.
